data.text/markdown:
When AI reads an old scanned table, does each number land in the right cell?

The fema-nrc-extraction-accuracy spike (issue #175) found that a vision model reading the page image finds 99.3% of the numbers printed on old NRC scans. "Found" there means the number appears somewhere in the transcript. A table is only useful if each number sits in its own row and column, so this notebook asks two things of the same saved answers:
  1. How far does "found" overstate "in the right cell"? Each pipeline is scored both ways, side by side.
  2. Can the totals printed on the page catch the misplaced and misread numbers without an answer key? Where a table prints a total, we add up the extracted column and compare.
Everything here rescores answers that spike saved. No model is called and nothing is downloaded.

How the source spike scored

The issue asked us to check this first, because if the spike already graded by cell, there's nothing to re-score.
  • FIS tables: already by cell. 2_long_vs_short.py pairs each key row with the answer row that agrees with it most (the location counts double), then compares column by column. A number in the wrong row or column counts as wrong. Below we add a "found anywhere" score next to it to show the gap.
  • NRC pages: not by cell. nrc_key.json is a flat list of the numbers on each page, and an answer was scored by how many of those numbers appear anywhere in its transcript. That's the 99.3%. A number in the wrong row still counted. The spike's README says so: "A number found in the wrong place still counts as found."
So the NRC side needs a key that says where each number goes.

The data: which keyed pages hold a table, and which print a total

The NRC key covers one page drawn at random from each of 10 reports. Only 4 of those pages are tables. The other 6 are two reference lists, a table of contents, a page of prose, a page of figures and a references page set in two columns. We keyed rows and columns for the 4 tables (5 tables in all, since one page holds two) in nrc_cell_key.json: each row is a pattern that finds its label in a transcript, and the values printed in it, left to right. The FIS key is already rows and columns: one Summary of Discharges table from each of 8 studies. The cell below checks the new key against the source key's numbers: every value we keyed should be among the numbers the source spike keyed for that page.

data.text/markdown: 2 of 13 keyed tables print a total, both on NRC pages: Table II on 5777799 (fuel leakage for 10 µ and 30 µ particles, and their total, for each case) and the 1981 dot-matrix pellet table on 1083928 (total UO2 weight and total fuel length under the table). FIS discharge tables print none: peak flows at different points on a river don't add up. That leaves 7 checkable columns, so the totals check below rests on very few columns. The pellet table has 60 rows and the source key covers rows 1-15. To score the totals we need the whole weight and length columns. Both image reads agree on all 600 values in rows 1-60, and their weight and length columns add up exactly to the printed totals, so we take that transcription as the truth for rows 16-60. We use those rows only for the totals check and leave them out of the accuracy scores, since scoring the image pipelines against their own reading would be circular.

Reading cells out of a transcript

The NRC answers are transcripts, not tables. The image pipeline was asked for "tables row by row" and mostly wrote Markdown tables. The two OCR-text pipelines were asked for "a clean transcription" and wrote lines of text. For each table we:
  1. cut the transcript down to the table (from its title to the note under it),
  2. find each row's label, and take the text from there up to the next row's label,
  3. read the values in that stretch left to right: numbers, ranges like 10-30, powers like 4.133x10-4, and printed placeholders such as -, ---, NA and *, which hold a column but aren't scored.
A value is in the right cell if it's the n-th value in its row, as printed. It is in the right row if it's anywhere in that row's stretch, and found if it's anywhere in the transcript, which is what the source spike measured. A wrong value is a wrong cell if its value is somewhere else in the transcript, a wrong digit if a different value sits in its place, and missing if nothing does.

Scoring the NRC tables

Six model pipelines from the source spike: the PDF's text layer, Tesseract's text or the page image, each read by Claude Haiku 5.5 and by Gemini 3.8 Flash. (The two no-model pipelines aren't saved as answers; they would need Tesseract and the PDFs, and they aren't AI reads.)

data.text/markdown: What this shows. Reading the image, Haiku put 100.0% (99-100) of the NRC table values in the right cell, against 100.0% (99-100) found. The gap is 0 cells. Through Tesseract's text the gap opens up: Haiku found 45.1% (39-51) but placed 34.3% (29-40). Most of the gap is values that landed in the right row but the wrong column, or in a different row, as OCR text loses the table's layout. Gemini's image read has no answer for 5777799: Gemini refused that page four times in the source spike (HTTP 502, "blocked the response: OTHER"), so its 99 values there count as missing. The intervals are Wilson 95% intervals that treat every cell as independent. They aren't: cells on one page share a scan and a layout, and there are only 4 pages, so the real uncertainty is wider than shown.

data.text/markdown: What this shows. On the scanned FIS tables the gap between found and right cell is 0 to 10 cells per pipeline. The page image put every value in its cell with both models. The text pipelines lose values outright (wrong digits and missing rows) more than they misplace them, because each FIS row is typed by the model into named fields, which keeps a value and its column together. The whole-study runs aren't given the page, so a few of their numbers come from elsewhere in the study.

The totals check

For each column with a printed total, add up the extracted values and compare with the extracted total. It passes if they agree to the last printed decimal. A column that can't be added up (a value is missing or isn't a number) fails too, since a reviewer would have to look at it. For the pellet table the length total is the sum of the mean of the two length readings (L-1 and L-2), which is how the printed 30.0435 adds up. Then we compare with the key: a column with any wrong value (a part or the total) should fail, and a column with every value right should pass.

data.text/markdown: What this shows. Of 42 column checks (7 columns times six pipelines), 33 had at least one wrong value, and the check flagged 33 of them. It missed 0, and raised 0 false alarms on the 9 columns that were right. Most of what it caught a reviewer would see anyway: whole rows missing, or a column where OCR turned every .4204 into .24204. The case it's for is the quiet one, and the pellet table has it twice. Reading Tesseract's text, Haiku misread 15 of the 60 weights by a digit or two (11.595 for 11.505), and the column added up to 702.865 g instead of the printed 704.091. Flash misread 8 and added up to 704.333. Every value there looks plausible on its own; only the sum gives them away. The check says a column is wrong, not which cell, and it rests on 7 columns from 2 tables. It can't see errors that leave the sum unchanged, such as two values swapped within a column.

What this doesn't show

  • Very few totals. 2 of 13 keyed tables and 7 columns print a total. The catch rate rests on those 7 columns read by six pipelines, which is 42 checks but far fewer independent cases.
  • Swaps within a column pass. If two values in one column trade places, the column still adds up. The check only sees errors that change a column's sum. Two errors that cancel out would also pass.
  • Tables with no totals get no check. None of the FIS discharge tables, the absorbent table or the fragility table print a total.
  • A small, AI-built key. Four NRC pages and eight FIS pages. The NRC number key was built by an AI worker, and the row/column key here was too, by eye from the page images. Rows 16-60 of the pellet table come from the two image reads (checked against the printed totals), not by eye.
  • The OCR-text pipelines weren't asked for a table. They were asked for a clean transcription, so their cell scores measure whether their output can be used as a table, not whether they followed an instruction to make one. Our row finder also only sees a row if its label survived OCR.
